question: Identify two types of organisational structure a business might use.

points: Hierarchical (1)
Flat (1)
Matrix (1)
Holacratic (1)

question: State one advantage and one disadvantage of a hierarchical structure.

points: Advantage: clear chain of command / clear lines of authority and accountability (1)
Disadvantage: slow communication / many layers slow decision-making (1)

question: Identify two functional areas of a business.

points: Human resources (1)
Marketing (1)
Finance (1)
Production / operations (1)
Sales (1)
Customer service (1)
Purchasing (1)
Research and development (1)

question: Explain the role of the human resources function in a business.

points: HR recruits, selects and trains staff (1) ensuring the business has the skilled workforce it needs (1)
HR manages pay, contracts, appraisals and disciplinary matters (1) and ensures employment law is followed (1)

question: Explain the role of the marketing function in a business.

points: Marketing identifies customer needs through market research (1) and develops products/services to meet them (1)
Marketing promotes products and manages the brand (1) to attract and retain customers and increase sales (1)

question: State two aims a private sector business might have.

points: Making profits / profit maximisation (1)
Survival (1)
Growth (1)
Market leadership (1)
Break-even (1)

question: State two aims a not-for-profit organisation might have.

points: Education (1)
Housing (1)
Alleviating poverty (1)
Healthcare (1)
Providing a service to members/community (1)

question: Identify what the acronym SMART stands for in relation to objectives.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1 mark for each correct element, up to 2.
points: Specific (1)
Measurable (1)
Achievable (1)
Relevant (1)
Time-constrained / Time-bound (1)

question: Explain why businesses set SMART objectives.

points: SMART objectives are specific and measurable (1) so progress can be tracked and success assessed (1)
They are achievable and relevant (1) so they are realistic and aligned with the business's overall aims (1)
Time-constrained objectives create urgency and focus (1) helping prioritise resources (1)

question: Explain the difference between the aims of a private business and a public sector organisation.

points: Private businesses typically aim to make profit and grow (1) to maximise returns for owners/shareholders (1)
Public sector organisations aim to provide services, control costs and give value for money (1) rather than generate profit (1)

scenario: TechNova Ltd is a fast-growing software company with 200 employees. It is considering moving from a hierarchical to a flatter structure.
question: Discuss whether TechNova Ltd should adopt a flatter organisational structure. (6)

indicative_content: Hierarchical: clear chain of command, defined roles, but slow decisions and poor communication across layers
Flat: fewer layers, faster communication, more employee empowerment, lower management costs
For a fast-growing tech firm, speed and innovation matter — flat structure supports agility
But 200 employees need coordination; too flat can create unclear reporting and overloaded managers
Could use a matrix or hybrid structure to combine flexibility with clarity
Conclusion: a flatter or matrix structure is likely beneficial but must retain clear accountability

level_descriptors.descriptor: Describes hierarchical vs flat in basic terms.
Compares advantages/disadvantages; links structure to TechNova's needs partially.
Thoroughly evaluates fit for a fast-growing tech business; justified recommendation.

question: Define the term 'span of control'.

points: The number of employees/subordinates who report directly to a manager (2)

question: Define the term 'chain of command'.

points: The line of authority and communication running from the top to the bottom of an organisation, showing who reports to whom (2)

question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of a flat organisational structure.

points: Advantage: fewer layers allow faster communication and decision-making (1) and reduce management costs (1)
Disadvantage: wide spans of control can overload managers (1) and provide less supervision and fewer promotion opportunities (1)

question: Explain what is meant by a matrix structure and when it might be used.

points: A matrix structure groups employees by both function and project (1) so staff report to more than one manager (1)
It is used for project-based work where cross-functional teams are needed (1) such as product development or consultancy (1)

question: Explain what is meant by a holacratic structure.

points: A holacratic structure removes traditional management hierarchy (1) distributing decision-making authority across self-managing teams/circles (1)
It gives employees autonomy and responsibility (1) and suits innovative, fast-moving organisations (1)

question: Explain the role of the finance function in a business.

points: Finance manages the business's money, budgets and accounts (1) ensuring bills are paid and cash flow is controlled (1)
It prepares financial statements, monitors costs and provides information for decision-making (1) supporting profitability and planning (1)

question: Explain the role of the production/operations function in a business.

points: Production/operations converts inputs into finished goods or services (1) managing the production process, quality and stock (1)
It aims to produce efficiently at the right cost and quality (1) to meet customer demand on time (1)

question: Explain the role of the sales function in a business.

points: Sales generates revenue by selling the business's products or services (1) identifying customers and closing deals (1)
It builds relationships with customers (1) and provides feedback on customer needs to other functions (1)

question: Explain the role of the customer service function.

points: Customer service handles enquiries, complaints and after-sales support (1) ensuring customers are satisfied (1)
Good customer service builds loyalty and repeat business (1) protecting the business's reputation (1)

question: Explain the role of research and development (R&D) in a business.

points: R&D develops new products and improves existing ones (1) helping the business innovate and stay competitive (1)
It tests and refines ideas before launch (1) reducing the risk of product failure (1)

question: Explain why different functional areas of a business need to work together.

points: Functions are interdependent — e.g. marketing must know what production can deliver (1) and finance must fund HR's recruitment (1)
Poor coordination between functions causes delays, duplication and conflicting decisions (1) so cooperation improves efficiency and performance (1)

question: Define the term 'aim' in a business context.

points: A long-term goal or purpose that a business works towards, setting its overall direction (2)

question: Define the term 'objective' in a business context.

points: A specific, measurable target that a business sets to help achieve its aims (2)

question: State two aims a public sector organisation might have.

points: Providing a quality service to the public (1)
Value for money (1)
Meeting social/community needs (1)
Operating within budget (1)
Providing universal access to services (1)

question: Explain why a business's aims and objectives may change over time.

points: Changes in the external environment (e.g. recession, new competitors) (1) may force a business to revise its aims to survive (1)
As a business grows, its aims evolve from survival to growth and market leadership (1) requiring new objectives (1)

question: Explain, using the SMART criteria, whether the objective 'to increase profit' is a good objective.

points: 'To increase profit' is not SMART because it is not specific, measurable or time-constrained (1) — it does not say by how much or by when (1)
A better objective would be 'to increase profit by 10% within 12 months' (1) which is specific, measurable and time-constrained (1)

question: Analyse why objectives should be achievable and relevant.

points: If objectives are not achievable they demotivate staff and are meaningless (1); unrealistic targets are ignored (1)
Relevant objectives align with the business's overall aims (1) so effort is focused on what matters for success (1)

scenario: ClearCo Ltd is a 300-employee manufacturer currently organised hierarchically, with aims to grow into new markets and improve innovation. It is reviewing its structure and objectives.
question: Evaluate how ClearCo Ltd could reorganise its structure and set objectives to support its growth and innovation aims. (12)

indicative_content: ClearCo's hierarchical structure is stable but may slow decision-making, hindering innovation
Options: flatten the hierarchy to speed communication, or adopt a matrix structure for cross-functional innovation projects
Functional areas (R&D, marketing, production) must coordinate to support growth into new markets
Aims (growth, innovation) should be translated into SMART objectives, e.g. 'launch 2 new products within 18 months'
Flatter/matrix structures empower staff and support creativity but require clear accountability at 300 employees
Balance: a hybrid structure retaining some hierarchy for control while adding project teams for innovation
Conclusion: a matrix or flatter structure with SMART, innovation-focused objectives best supports ClearCo's aims

level_descriptors.descriptor: Describes structure and objectives in basic terms.
Links structure/objectives to ClearCo's aims partially.
Balanced evaluation of structural options and objective-setting.
Thorough evaluation recommending a specific structure and SMART objectives with justification.

question: Identify two advantages of a hierarchical organisational structure.

points: Clear chain of command (1)
Clear lines of authority and accountability (1)
Clear promotion/career progression path (1)
Specialist roles and expertise at each level (1)

question: Identify two disadvantages of a hierarchical organisational structure.

points: Slow communication through many layers (1)
Slow decision-making (1)
Less flexible/responsive to change (1)
High management costs (1)
Employees may feel less empowered (1)

question: Explain how a wide span of control differs from a narrow span of control.

points: A wide span of control means a manager supervises many subordinates (1) common in flat structures (1)
A narrow span of control means a manager supervises few subordinates (1) common in tall/hierarchical structures (1)

question: Explain how organisational structure can affect communication within a business.

points: A hierarchical structure has many layers so messages pass through several levels (1) slowing communication and risking distortion (1)
A flat structure has few layers (1) so communication is faster and more direct (1)

question: Explain why a business might change from a hierarchical to a flatter structure.

points: To speed up communication and decision-making (1) by removing layers of management (1)
To reduce management costs (1) and empower employees (1)
To become more flexible and responsive to change (1)

question: Identify the functional area responsible for buying raw materials and supplies.

points: Purchasing (or procurement) (2)

question: Explain the role of the purchasing function in a business.

points: Purchasing sources and buys the raw materials, components and supplies the business needs (1) at the right quality and price (1)
It manages supplier relationships and negotiates terms (1) ensuring reliable supply and good value (1)

question: Explain the role of the IT function in a modern business.

points: IT maintains the business's computer systems, networks and software (1) ensuring they run reliably and securely (1)
It supports other functions through technology (1) e.g. e-commerce, data analysis and communication tools (1)

question: Explain the role of the administration function in a business.

points: Administration provides clerical and support services (1) such as record-keeping, filing and correspondence (1)
It ensures the smooth running of the organisation (1) by coordinating information and routine tasks (1)

question: Explain the difference between an aim and an objective, using an example.

points: An aim is a broad, long-term goal (e.g. 'to become the market leader') (1); an objective is a specific, measurable step towards it (e.g. 'to increase market share by 5% within a year') (1)
Objectives are more detailed and time-bound than aims (1) and are used to measure progress (1)

question: Explain why survival is often the first aim of a new business.

points: New businesses face high start-up costs and uncertain demand (1) and many fail in their first years (1)
Establishing a stable customer base and cash flow (1) is essential before pursuing growth or profit (1)

question: Explain how profit and growth as aims can conflict.

points: Pursuing profit in the short term may mean not investing in growth (1) reducing long-term expansion (1)
Pursuing growth requires heavy investment (1) which reduces short-term profit (1)
A business must balance the two aims over time (1)

question: Identify whether 'to increase sales by 15% in the next six months' is a SMART objective, explaining why.

points: Yes — it is specific (increase sales), measurable (15%), achievable/relevant (sales growth) and time-constrained (six months) (2)

question: Explain the benefit to a business of setting time-constrained objectives.

points: Time-constrained objectives create a deadline (1) which focuses effort and prioritises resources (1)
They allow progress to be reviewed at a set point (1) enabling corrective action if the business is off track (1)

scenario: FreshBrew is a growing coffee shop chain with 40 outlets. It currently uses a hierarchical structure but wants to improve innovation and respond faster to local customer needs.
question: Discuss whether FreshBrew should move to a flatter organisational structure. (6)

indicative_content: Hierarchical structure provides clear control across 40 outlets but may slow decisions and responsiveness
Flat structure would speed communication and empower outlet managers to respond to local needs
A flat structure reduces management layers and costs but may weaken central control and consistency
With 40 outlets, some hierarchy is needed for coordination and brand consistency
Alternative: decentralise decision-making to regional/outlet managers while keeping a slim hierarchy
Conclusion: a flatter structure with empowered outlet managers supports innovation and responsiveness, but FreshBrew should retain clear accountability

level_descriptors.descriptor: Describes hierarchical vs flat in basic terms.
Compares the structures with partial application to FreshBrew's 40 outlets.
Thoroughly evaluates fit for a multi-outlet chain; justified recommendation.

question: Explain what is meant by the term 'delegation' in an organisation.

points: Delegation is passing authority and responsibility for a task to a subordinate (1) while retaining overall accountability (1)
It empowers employees and frees managers' time (1) but requires trust and clear instructions (1)

question: Explain what is meant by 'centralisation' and 'decentralisation'.

points: Centralisation means decision-making is concentrated at the top of the organisation (1) giving senior managers control (1)
Decentralisation means decision-making is delegated to lower levels or branches (1) allowing faster local decisions (1)

question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of decentralisation.

points: Advantage: decisions are made closer to customers (1) enabling faster, better-informed responses (1)
Disadvantage: loss of central control and consistency (1) may lead to conflicting decisions across the business (1)

question: Explain how the marketing and production functions need to coordinate.

points: Marketing must promote products that production can actually deliver (1) to avoid promising more than the business can supply (1)
Production needs marketing's demand forecasts (1) to plan output levels and avoid over- or under-production (1)

question: Explain how the HR and finance functions need to coordinate.

points: Finance must provide the budget for HR to recruit and pay staff (1) ensuring wage costs are affordable (1)
HR provides finance with staff numbers and payroll data (1) needed for budgeting and financial planning (1)

question: Explain why larger businesses have more specialist functional areas.

points: Larger businesses have more complex operations (1) requiring specialist expertise in each area (1)
Specialisation improves efficiency and quality (1) but can create coordination challenges between functions (1)

question: Explain what is meant by 'market leadership' as a business aim.

points: Market leadership means being the business with the largest market share in its industry (1) (1)
It brings benefits such as economies of scale, brand recognition and pricing power (1) but requires significant growth and investment (1)

question: Explain why a business might aim to break even in its first year.

points: Breaking even (covering all costs) is a realistic first-year target (1) before the business is established enough to make a profit (1)
Achieving break-even ensures survival (1) which is the priority for a new business (1)

question: Explain the difference between profit maximisation and profit satisficing.

points: Profit maximisation means aiming for the highest possible profit (1) often the main aim of private businesses (1)
Profit satisficing means aiming for a satisfactory/acceptable level of profit (1) while pursuing other aims such as growth or work-life balance (1)

question: Explain why objectives should be measurable.

points: Measurable objectives allow progress to be tracked against a target (1) so the business knows whether it is succeeding (1)
Without measurement, it is impossible to judge performance (1) or take corrective action when falling short (1)

question: Explain why objectives should be relevant to the business.

points: Relevant objectives align with the business's overall aims and strategy (1) so effort is directed at what matters (1)
Irrelevant objectives waste resources (1) and do not move the business towards its goals (1)

question: Analyse how a business's objectives support the achievement of its aims.

points: Objectives break broad aims into specific, measurable steps (1) making progress towards the aim trackable (1)
Achieving a series of objectives cumulatively moves the business towards its overall aim (1) e.g. growth objectives support a growth aim (1)

scenario: A medium-sized charity with 80 staff currently has a flat structure but is struggling with unclear responsibilities and overworked managers.
question: Discuss whether the charity should introduce a more hierarchical structure. (6)

indicative_content: The flat structure causes unclear responsibilities and overworked managers (wide spans of control)
A hierarchical structure would clarify the chain of command and accountability
More layers would reduce each manager's span of control, easing workload
But hierarchy adds management costs and slows communication
For a charity, minimising overheads matters, but clear accountability is essential for effectiveness
Conclusion: a modest hierarchy (adding a middle management layer) balances clarity with cost, but the charity should avoid over-layering

level_descriptors.descriptor: Describes the two structures in basic terms.
Compares them with partial application to the charity's problems.
Thoroughly evaluates the trade-off between clarity and cost; justified recommendation.

question: State the difference between a tall and a flat organisational structure.

points: Tall: many layers of management and a long chain of command (1)
Flat: few layers and a short chain of command (1)

question: Identify the functional area responsible for advertising and promoting products.

points: Marketing (2)

question: Identify two aims a social enterprise might have.

points: Addressing a social or environmental problem (1)
Providing employment for disadvantaged groups (1)
Reinvesting profits into the social mission (1)
Financial sustainability (1)

question: Explain why objectives should be specific.

points: Specific objectives are clear and unambiguous (1) so everyone knows exactly what is expected (1)
Vague objectives are hard to act on and measure (1) reducing their usefulness for planning and control (1)
